docs.text: Hakus technical VTubing Guide Good morning everyone! This docummentation is segmented in multiple topics. Some topics may cross reference each other. Do not worry, I try to keep things simple and not explain each eventuality. Expect things to just work. I will use vocabulary instead of explaining things, but for many things, you can find an article from the search on the left. 3D VS 2D 2D VTubing is easy, quick and gives you a lot of creative freedom for your own designs. On the other hand 3d VTubing is complicated, painful and breaks all the time. If you just want to play some random desktop games a 2d VTubing model is probably best for you. You can get some good fake 3D effects with Live2D. But for some very specific instances investing into a 3D VTubing model might be cheaper and easier. If you play BeatSaber or VRChat 3D is not optional. If you are interested in 3D VTubing skip ahead to Basics for 3D VTubing

docs.text: Basics for 3D VTubing When it comes to 3d VTubing there are multiple ways you can approach this. Comission a custom 3D VTubing model Create your own model in blender Use VRoid to create an avatar Buy what you need on a market place Each of these approaches has advantages and disadvantages and what you should choose depends on how much time, money and skill you have or are able to acquire. Comissioning a 3D VTubing model Comissioning a 3D Model is the most expensive option out of all of these. You have to do nothing but imagine what you want. If you have no idea what you want I recommend you not going this path. The result you can get with this are pretty good for the effort you need to do, but its not very flexible. You will be stuck with whatever result you get out of this for a long time. And if there is something you'd like to have changed you most likely need to comission the change too. You buy a finished product. Creating your own model in blender This one costs you absolutely nothing. Except for your time. In theory there is no upper limit of what you can do. Everything is depending on how good you can handle the program, the technique and the art. You need need to learn how to model, rig, texture. You need to learn how to make the model in a way other programs can understand it. And if you are honest with yourself: the result will likely look mediocre or even bad. This option should be picked by creative people with thousands of hours available for their projects. Modeling 10 hours on weekends will likely not yield good results and probably frustrate you and make you give up. Please do not overestimate the complexity of this as you will likely learn all the incompatibilities after you have already invested a lot of time into this. This is a path you can go after you already understand how everything works and can be built from scratch. VRoid This option is the easiest one and the cheapest one to get a simple model out. You drag some sliders to modify your body shape, put on some pre made clothes, modify some textures and export your file as .VRM file. The .VRM file is a standardized file format specifically for models made in Roid. It is free and straight forward to use. But you will be limited to what this toolset offers you. If you can paint textures you will get pretty far with this and you have the option to purchase some clothing too. The program differentiates between different types of clothes (like dress, underweaer or shoes) so you can combine things how you want to. The .VRM format is supported by all major softwares (except for VR Chat, but that does not stop you from importing it there too). Marketplace avatar With this you buy your components from a market place. Two major marketplaces are currently available for purchasing components Jinxxy (little bit Furry targeted) BOOTH (japanese only) With this approach you essentially purchase an avatar base, look up clothes that fit your chosen avatar base and slap them on. Exporting to VR Chat is trivial as this approach is VR Chat native, but exporting for other programs requires some extra effort. This is the approach I recommend for the best results for beginners.

docs.text: Making an Avatar from Marketplace Components. With this approach you get the ease of making a premade avatar like in vroid or sims combined with the limits that unity offers. Generally this is targeted as VRChat avatars, but fear not. They can be ported into all applications and even into .VRM. The costs of this will be around 100$. This is neither the lower nor upper ceiling. This is just what you should have available to play around with. In general the process is picking an avatar base you like, picking some hair, picking an outfit and editing the textures before you export the avatar. Doing 3D modelling is possible but not required (for some parts like the avatar base I actually advice against editing it). Which market place to choose? There are generally only two options viable right now: Jinxxy and BOOTH. Which one you pick is simple. If you want a human avatar pick BOOTH. If you want an animal/Furry avatar pick Jinxxy. I don't have experience with furry avatars myself, but please feel free to write an article about this yourself. The remaining documentation will be targeted specifically for human avatars. But I can imagine that the things you do are just the same with a few tools not being available to use. Choosing your Avatar Base Woah wait a minute, are you not gonna explain things first? No! Because there is not much you need to know beside that I describe in this topic. For choosing the avatar I recommend https://boothplorer.com/avatars for english natives. Japanese natives might be able to find their way round https://booth.pm but boothplorer also offers the ability to find clothes that fit your avatar base easily. Please keep in mind that boothplorer is a third party tool and scrapes data. Therefore you should always verify the information you see on the original page. Even if you translate the entire page from japanese to english. // TODO: insert Screenshot of boothplorer You can find outfits matching your avatar directly under the avatar in boothplorer. Chibi Avatars For chibi avatars there are two options viable. They are viable because they have already a ton of clothes and add-ons available that natively fit for their model. Kipfel (>10k items) https://boothplorer.com/avatar/5813187 Mamehimita (>8k items) https://boothplorer.com/avatar/4340548 Male Avatars There are a few Male bases available, but the available outfits are very limited. You might need to retexture some items to make your model unique. If you don't care about that and just want to assemble something that works you should still keep in mind that none of the male characters have >1k items to chose from.
